newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian Uralmash says in cash crunch.
newsitem.headline: Russian Uralmash says in cash crunch.

text.p: One of Russia's biggest employers, Uralmash, said on Friday it was caught in a liquidity crisis with debts to workers and the government of 160 billion roubles, ($29.5 million) -- but it is owed 220 billion roubles in turn.
Yury Platonov, Moscow representative of the machine-building firm, said a government tax squeeze had caused a liquidity crisis, threatening the company more than two years of inflation.
"For the last year or two, the factory has been able to muddle through, but now our metal industry clients cannot pay us, and so we have no money to pay workers," he said.

Uralmash, based in the Urals city of Yekaterinburg, owes its 18,000 workers 23 billion roubles and the government 137 billion roubles, he said, adding that he himself had not been paid for over two months.
Russia has ordered industrial enterprises to pay taxes before other debts, which firms including Uralmash say effectively requires them to not pay wages or bills.
OAO Uralsky Zavod Tyazhelogo Mashinostroyeniya, says it cannot pay bills because clients cannot pay theirs.
But President Boris Yeltsin said on Thursday big companies who refuse to pay taxes are holding up wage payments to public sector workers.

"Students, teachers, the military and other workers in the state sphere are not receiving wages because a number of big enterprises are literally taking the finances of the country by the throat and refusing to pay taxes," he said in a statment.
Russian firms used to liquidity problems have developed complicated barter networks, and some have sold their own debt in the form of negotiable instruments to keep in business.
But Platonov said Uralmash loses up to 40 percent of the value of payments made in kind as it carries out trades to come up with the cash or goods the firm wants.
"The biggest problem is cash money -- liquidity. Uralmash is not a trading firm," he said.
He said the factory, which is working at less than half capacity, had orders but was unable to fill all of them for lack of capital.
"We need 33 percent of the cost of the product for materials and electricity," he said. $1= 5,424 roubles
